newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African union boss wants tax on rich in budget.
newsitem.headline: S.African union boss wants tax on rich in budget.

text.p: South Africa's most powerful trade unionist, Sam Shilowa, called on the government on Friday to increase taxes on the rich, on business and on luxury goods in the budget on March 12, and to focus less on the deficit.

Shilowa, general secretary of the Confederation of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), said in an article for the Sowetan newspaper that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel should set a 55 percent tax rate on the super rich, whom he did not define.
South African workers, who say they are among the world's most heavily taxed, pay a top rate of 45 percent on income over 100,000 rand, though few come into this bracket.
He also criticised Manuel's concentration in a macroeconomic plan unveiled last year on a pledge to cut the budget deficit from 5.1 percent this year to four percent in 1997/98.

"Budget deficit management is not a mathematical equation. It will result in a cut in social spending, choke the economy and destroy jobs," said Shilowa, who called for higher tax to fund higher social spending.
Cosatu is officially allied to President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress but friction between them has grown over the government's market-friendly economic policies.
Shilowa called for the introduction of capital gains tax, a higher rate of VAT on luxury goods, higher corporate tax and closure of loopholes used by the wealthy to reduce tax liability.

Companies should pay a levy on profits of perhaps five percent to fund public works. Spending on housing, health and education should rise if the government is serious about cutting gaping inequalities in post-apartheid South Africa, he said.
"South Africa is one of the most unequal societies in the world," Shilowa said.
One of the biggest divisions is between those in jobs and the unemployed, and Shilowa said Cosatu would judge the budget primarily on its success in creating new jobs and preserving existing ones.
